  Embedded two-dimensional LiDAR localization must combine accuracy,
  disturbance recovery, and bounded resource use. This work deploys a

  sessions; auxiliary host and RV1106 evidence is explicitly identified.

# Introduction

Reliable localization on a constrained embedded platform is not established by pose
accuracy alone. The implementation must track through physical motion, detect
loss, recover after relocation, tolerate temporary scan disturbance, and meet
the sensor period with limited CPU and memory. We address these requirements
on an RV1103 board–LiDAR platform using one production implementation and one traceable
evaluation chain.

Correlative scan matching, coarse-to-fine search, and global relocalization
are established concepts. Their combination is useful on embedded hardware
because local search exploits the previous pose, global search removes that
assumption after displacement, and a likelihood pyramid limits exhaustive
fine-resolution work. Our novelty claim is therefore not a new matching
equation. It is the implemented local–global multi-resolution co-design and
its joint evaluation through physical, factor-isolation, and sensor-paced
hardware evidence. All reported performance values are computed from the
finalized project evidence.

This paper asks whether the production method (i) maintains route tracking,
(ii) recovers from same- and cross-room kidnapping, (iii) remains usable
during short dynamic obstruction, (iv) requires both global and
multi-resolution factors, and (v) fits the RV1103 CPU, memory, and 100 ms scan
budget. The contributions are:

1. a five-state embedded tracker combining bounded local search,
   whole-map recovery, and multi-resolution refinement;
2. six enforced protocols covering Ground Truth, Route, Kidnapped, Dynamic
   Occluded, Ablation, and Resource evaluation, with RV1103 as the primary
   target and auxiliary evidence identified by execution target; and
3. finalized, version-controlled, checksum-verifiable evidence binding
   telemetry, configuration, map/binary hashes, processed metrics, and
   manifests across 24 reported sessions.

# Related Work

Recent 2D LiDAR SLAM literature spans matching, filtering, graph optimization,
sensor fusion, and dynamic-scene handling [@ran2025review]. Robust front ends
and probabilistic estimators address ambiguous geometry
[@huang2022robust2d; @lim2024minimax], while improved Gmapping and tightly
coupled LiDAR–inertial–wheel systems add complementary motion constraints
[@tian2023gmapping; @zhang2024_2dliw]. Indoor mapping and sparse sensing have
also been treated through conditional line fitting and efficient graph
optimization [@prieto2024weighted; @zhou2022sparse]. Visual loop closure can
disambiguate similar indoor geometry [@zhou2023visual], and cross-environment
evaluation shows that reported SLAM performance depends on scene structure
and test conditions [@li2024evaluation].

Computational efficiency remains central to deployable LiDAR estimation.
Recent work demonstrates carefully engineered point registration, continuous
scan slicing, and FPGA acceleration [@vizzo2023kiss; @karimi2021lola;
@sugiura2021fpga]. Global localization can also be formulated through learned
scan similarity [@chen2022overlapnet]. Dynamic-scene studies instead detect
scan-matching faults, identify moving objects, or modify matching to tolerate
occlusion [@jeong2023fault; @mihalik2022dynamic; @koyama2026occlusion].
These studies motivate the present combination: robust 2D matching informs
the fixed-map front end [@huang2022robust2d], multi-resolution and engineered
registration motivate bounded search [@vizzo2023kiss; @sugiura2021fpga], and
dynamic-scene studies motivate explicit rejection and recovery rather than
unsupported object classification [@jeong2023fault; @mihalik2022dynamic;
@koyama2026occlusion]. The remaining gap addressed here is their joint
deployment and evaluation: fixed-map 2D localization, whole-map recovery,
physical disturbance, controlled factor isolation, and sensor-paced resource
measurement on a 64 MiB target within one traceable workflow.

# System and Production Method

The primary target is a Luckfox Pico Plus RV1103 with 64 MiB DDR2, 128 MiB
SPI NAND, Buildroot/Linux 5.10.160, and a YDLIDAR T-mini Plus connected by
UART at 230400 bit/s [@luckfox_rv1103; @ydlidar_tmini_plus]. The LiDAR
operates at 10 Hz and 4 kHz ranging; valid localization ranges are
0.05–12 m, making 100 ms the nominal scan-cycle deadline. RV1106 is reported
only where physical evidence exists [@luckfox_rv1106]; comparisons are
restricted to conditions represented on both targets. The RV1103 and RV1106
deployments use independently acquired map and marker-reference realizations,
so cross-board results are descriptive deployment comparisons, not isolated
hardware benchmarks.

For a candidate pose, valid scan endpoints are transformed into the map and
scored against a likelihood field. A candidate requires at least the larger
of three points or one third of the scan inside the map and must meet the 0.90
acceptance threshold. Local tracking searches ±0.50 m and ±0.35 rad around
the last accepted pose using 0.05 m and 1° finest increments. Global recovery
searches the complete coarse map at 10° heading steps, retains the best 12
candidates, and refines each through progressively finer likelihood levels.

The state machine exposes uncertainty rather than silently propagating a poor
pose. `GLOBAL_SEARCH` acquires an initial or replacement pose; acceptance
enters `RECOVERED`; three accepted local updates confirm `TRACKING`. One or
two rejected scans produce `DEGRADED`; the third produces `LOST`, invalidates
the local center, and triggers whole-map search. A false recovery is a return
to `LOST` before confirmed tracking. The deployed configuration,
`local_global_multi`, is shared by live UART localization and deterministic
replay through the same tracker, score, map representation, and transitions.

The dashboard, backend, and firmware enforce one session lifecycle:
preflight verifies target state and map/binary SHA-256 hashes; session creation
freezes configuration and references; capture isolates the experimental
localizer; scenario events are order-checked; stop copies evidence with
checksums and restores normal localization; analysis validates protocol
structure; finalization creates an inventory and manifest. Raw scans are
streamed to the backend when board storage would be unsafe. Reviewed evidence
is finalized, version-controlled, and checksum-verifiable; it can later be
replayed without rewriting the physical run.

# Experimental Method

## Environment and protocols

The primary RV1103 occupancy grid is 148 × 122 pixels at 0.05 m/pixel. Eight
surveyed locations define reciprocal routes: R1 traverses the physical
locations M1→M8 and R2 traverses them in reverse. Acquisition files number
each route by travel order, however, so R2/M\(k\) means the \(k\)-th checkpoint
of the reverse traversal rather than the same physical location as R1/M\(k\).
Furniture-change trials deliberately retain their frozen localization map
while the physical arrangement differs. The separately acquired changed-scene
grid documents the disturbance but is not used for localization. All route
movement and kidnapped repositioning were performed manually with the
board–LiDAR assembly; no drive base, motor controller, or autonomous
navigation stack was integrated.

@tbl-protocols gives the complete experimental logic without repeating
the common session lifecycle. Ground Truth, Route, Kidnapped, and Dynamic
Occluded are physical tests. Host Ablation is identical-scan unpaced replay;
board Ablation validates only the selected production method. Resource
testing separates live idle/tracking and recorded-timestamp replay.

| Test | Controlled execution | Validity gate and primary measures |
|---|---|---|
| Ground Truth | Independently return the board–LiDAR assembly to one surveyed M1 pose ten times. | Exactly 10 records; pose repeatability. |
| Route | Move the board–LiDAR assembly manually through eight ordered checkpoints in R1 and R2; nominal, static 90° LiDAR occlusion, or changed furniture. | 8 unique ordered poses; position and wrapped-heading error. |
| Kidnapped | Stabilize the localization assembly at A, cover and relocate it, then uncover it at B; same- or cross-room. | One start/release/final pose, 60 s timeout; first recovery, stable tracking, final error, false recovery. |
| Dynamic Occluded | Keep the localization assembly stationary at M2–M7 while a 13 × 13 × 30 cm object crosses about 0.50 m ahead for 4 s. | Six 3.5–4.5 s windows and eight checkpoints; acceptance, drift, recovery, and near-sector response. |
| Ablation | On the host, replay each source through a 2×2 method design; on RV1103, validate only the selected method. Map, initial pose, scan sequence, hash, and timestamps remain equal among variants of a source. | Expected variant set and equal within-source input; recovery, acceptance, and matcher cost. |
| Resource | RV1103 live idle/R1/R2 and recorded-paced replay. | Complete CPU/RSS/latency fields; boundary-specific overruns and recovery. |

: Six test families and their enforced evidence. {#tbl-protocols}

Dynamic evidence counts returns at 0.30–0.80 m in left (+10° to +65°), center
(−10° to +10°), and right (−65° to −10°) sectors relative to the preceding
one-second baseline. A crossing is valid without occupying all sectors; a
stricter auxiliary direction detector requires at least three excess points
in each sector with ordered peaks.

## Measures and traceability

Position error is $e_p=\sqrt{(\hat{x}-x)^2+(\hat{y}-y)^2}$; heading error is
the absolute wrapped angle
$e_\theta=|\operatorname{atan2}(\sin(\hat\theta-\theta),
\cos(\hat\theta-\theta))|$. Reports use RMSE, P95, maximum, success
proportions, and recovery latency. For live runs, an overrun is an observed
inter-scan cycle above 100 ms and therefore includes sensor transport, I/O,
and scheduling. For recorded-paced replay, a computation-deadline miss is
matcher execution above 100 ms; pacing wait is recorded separately. These
rates characterize different execution boundaries and are not directly
interchangeable.
Results remain descriptive because sessions are limited and temporally
dependent. The 24 reported sessions comprise one Ground Truth, eight Route,
seven Kidnapped, two Dynamic Occluded, four Ablation, and two Resource
sessions. Short test/source labels replace filesystem paths and long
identifiers in the paper; the manifest preserves the exact mapping.

# Results

## Ground Truth

Ground Truth produced exactly ten records at M1. Position RMSE was
0.000017 m and heading RMSE/max was 0.570°/1.342°. The repeated discrete pose
must not be interpreted as micrometre surveying accuracy; it verifies
estimator/reference repeatability at one marker. This Accepted test exists
only for RV1106, so no RV1103–RV1106 comparison is made.

## Route

| Platform | Condition | Route | Success | Position RMSE / P95 (m) | Heading RMSE / P95 (°) |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| RV1103 | Nominal | R1 | 8/8 | 0.031 / 0.050 | 0.632 / 0.836 |
| RV1103 | Nominal | R2 | 8/8 | 0.025 / 0.050 | 0.542 / 0.795 |
| RV1106 | Nominal | R1 | 8/8 | 0.040 / 0.050 | 1.697 / 3.081 |
| RV1106 | Nominal | R2 | 8/8 | 0.040 / 0.050 | 2.588 / 3.812 |
| RV1106 | Furniture changed | R1 | 8/8 | 0.043 / 0.063 | 1.940 / 3.637* |
| RV1106 | Furniture changed | R2 | 8/8 | 0.031 / 0.050 | 1.298 / 2.293* |
| RV1106 | Static 90° occlusion | R1 | 8/8 | 0.064 / 0.090 | 1.926 / 3.646 |
| RV1106 | Static 90° occlusion | R2 | 8/8 | 0.059 / 0.071 | 1.935 / 3.206 |

: Physical Route results. *Post-hoc corrected reference heading; estimator
output and Accepted evidence were not changed. {#tbl-route}

RV1103 nominal performance pooled over both directions was 0.0279 m position
RMSE and 0.589° heading RMSE, with 16/16 valid checkpoints. The only
cross-board Route comparison uses nominal R1/R2, which exists on both targets:
RV1106 also achieved 16/16, with pooled 0.0396 m position RMSE and 2.189°
heading RMSE. Static occlusion and furniture change exist only on RV1106 and
are therefore reported as RV1106 disturbance results, not compared with
RV1103. Because the platforms used independently acquired map and marker
references, the pooled errors describe two deployments and do not isolate a
hardware effect. Static occlusion retained 16/16 valid checkpoints. Furniture
change
also retained 16/16; its raw heading RMSE near 111° arose from an
operator-entered reference heading. One shared +111.023° correction was
applied only in secondary analysis: independently observed R1/R2 offsets were
110.804° and 111.241° (difference 0.436°), yielding corrected RMSE of 1.940°
and 1.298°. This supports internally consistent localization under the
frozen-map mismatch, but the shared correction was estimated and evaluated on
the same records without a holdout. The corrected residuals therefore show
internal consistency, not independently validated absolute-heading accuracy.

## Kidnapped

| Platform | Scenario | Trials | First recovery (ms) | Stable tracking (ms) | Maximum final error |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| RV1103 | Same room | 2 | 529–970 | 778–1,132 | 0.0002 m / 0.420° |
| RV1103 | Cross room | 2 | 790–952 | 1,034–1,201 | 0.0501 m / 0.268° |
| RV1106 | Same room | 1 | 438 | 622 | 0.0500 m / 2.392° |
| RV1106 | Cross room | 2 | 344–779 | 530–963 | 0.0501 m / 1.642° |

: Physical Kidnapped recovery. Every trial succeeded within 60 s.
{#tbl-kidnapped}

RV1103 recovered all four displacements; mean first/stable latency was
810/1,036 ms. RV1106 recovered all three; corresponding means were 520/705 ms.
For the balanced cross-room subset (two trials per target), RV1103 first/stable
means were 871/1,118 ms and RV1106 means were 562/747 ms; all four cross-room
trials succeeded. Same-room results remain listed but are not used for a
balanced comparison because RV1103 has two trials and RV1106 one. These
descriptive observations do not establish universal platform superiority.

## Dynamic Occluded

| Route | Events | Accepted scans | Post-event tracking mean / P95 | Position / heading RMSE |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| R1 | 6 | 242/242 (100%) | 64.5 / 92.3 ms | 0.035 m / 0.952° |
| R2 | 6 | 230/233 (98.71%) | 52.2 / 91.5 ms | 0.017 m / 0.474° |

: RV1103 Dynamic Occluded session summary. {#tbl-dynamic}

All 12 planned windows lasted 4.000–4.002 s. Overall acceptance was 472/475
(99.37%); maximum window drift was 0.050 m and 1.465°. Eleven events remained
continuously accepted. R2/M4 briefly reached `LOST` and recovered without
operator intervention. Because this event has neither near-sector excess nor
beam-level raw scans, a door-state or other map mismatch is plausible but
unverified. The supported result is automatic confidence detection and
recovery, not causal attribution. The strict direction detector confirmed
only 2/12 passages, so the experiment supports localization robustness to
short stationary crossings, not general obstacle-motion recognition or
avoidance.

returns above the preceding one-second baseline; a dash means no positive
excess. The black dots around M2–M7 in Panel A are evidence-derived schematic
projections. At each marker, the R1 or R2 event with the largest total sector
excess is shown; every non-zero side is retained even when the response occurs
in only one sector. Dot count is scaled for readability. These are not raw
beam endpoints because beam-level scan rows were not captured.
R2/M4 accepted 30/33 scans: scores 0.917–0.996 were accepted, while
0.897, 0.884, and 0.891 were rejected at the 0.90 threshold. The third
rejection caused `LOST`; global acceptance followed after 935 ms and confirmed
tracking after 1.087 s. Its absent near-sector signal prevents attribution to
the moving object.](figures/dynamic-occlusion-evidence.svg){#fig-dynamic-occlusion width=95% fig-pos="H"}

## Ablation

Host replay evaluated local/global search and single/multi-resolution as a
2×2 design. Abbreviations are L-S (local single), L-M (local multi), LG-S
(local–global single), and LG-M (local–global multi). S1 is an RV1106
cross-room Kidnapped source; S2 is an RV1103 same-room Kidnapped source; and
S3 is an RV1103 cross-room Kidnapped source. Equal-input control applies among
the four host variants within S1 or within S2. Board validation reuses S2 and
S3 but executes only LG-M.

| Target/source | Variant | Accepted | Recovery | Matcher P95 (ms) | Recovery (ms) |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Host/S1 | L-S | 35.26% | No | 92.79 | — |
| Host/S1 | L-M | 77.32% | No | 4.17 | — |
| Host/S1 | LG-S | 77.32% | No | 3,489.69 | — |
| Host/S1 | LG-M | 98.56% | Yes | 5.57 | 365 |
| Host/S2 | L-S | 82.03% | No | 108.21 | — |
| Host/S2 | L-M | 82.03% | No | 5.17 | — |
| Host/S2 | LG-S | 82.03% | No | 3,023.47 | — |
| Host/S2 | LG-M | 98.23% | Yes | 4.11 | 985 |
| RV1103/S2 | LG-M | 98.23% | Yes | 50.06 | 985 |
| RV1103/S3 | LG-M | 98.78% | Yes | 49.35 | 1,045 |

: Identical-input host ablation and selected-method RV1103 validation.
{#tbl-ablation}

Only LG-M recovered in both factorial sources. Multi-resolution reduced
local-only mean matcher time from 67.66 to 3.02 ms (S1) and 71.15 to 3.43 ms
(S2). Global search without the pyramid was computationally prohibitive and
still failed the recovery criterion. The interaction is operationally clear:
global search supplies recovery, while multi-resolution makes it tractable.
RV1103 replay reproduced the selected method's acceptance and recovery with
1,420–1,436 KiB peak RSS. Host CPU near 100% represents unpaced computation
and is not compared with board utilization.

## Resource

| Mode | Duration / observations | Accepted | CPU mean (%) | RSS peak (KiB) | Matcher or tracking P95 (ms) | Cycle P95 / overruns |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Live idle | 63.1 s / 63 | — | 0.57 | 1,688 | — | — |
| Live R1 | 61.4 s / 582 | 100% | 60.89 | 2,076 | 62.93 | 105.31 / 21.13% |
| Live R2 | 62.4 s / 626 | 100% | 60.96 | 2,076 | 62.93 | 105.53 / 21.41% |
| Paced replay | 576 scans | 98.78% | 66.05* | 1,456 | 67.25 | 4/576 (0.69%) |

: Live and recorded-paced RV1103 resource results. Idle observations are
one-second resource samples; all other observations are localization scans.
The replay value marked * is time-weighted CPU. Live overruns and replay
computation-deadline misses use the distinct boundaries defined in the
Experimental Method.
{#tbl-resource}

Live R1/R2 accepted every scan without `LOST` or `DEGRADED`. Their cycle P95
was 105–106 ms and about one fifth of cycles exceeded 100 ms, demonstrating
limited scheduling margin.

Recorded-paced cross-room replay contained complete resource telemetry for
576/576 rows. Matcher-active CPU mean/P95 was 98.42/99.94%, whereas
time-weighted CPU was 66.05% because it includes inter-scan waiting. Tracking
latency mean/P95/max was 50.96/67.25/107.71 ms; global latency mean/max was
866.24/1,110.28 ms. The replay recovered in 1.045 s with three global scans,
0.04998 m/0.343° final error, and zero false recoveries. Routine tracking
therefore fits the recorded 100 ms pacing, while global recovery dominates
worst-case latency.

# Discussion

The physical and continuous results answer the five research questions
consistently. Nominal tracking is centimetre-scale at all checkpoints;
confirmed Kidnapped recovery completes in about one second on RV1103.
Dynamic trials support localization through short crossings, not object
classification or avoidance.

Ablation supplies the mechanism behind these results. Local-only variants
cannot resolve displacement; global single-resolution search is too costly;
only the joint global and multi-resolution configuration provides recovery
with tractable computation. Hardware replay separates near-100%
matcher-active CPU from 66.05% time-weighted CPU. The live approximately 20%
inter-scan overrun rate exposes sensor, I/O, and scheduling costs outside the
replay computation boundary; it must not be read as a direct contrast with
the replay's 0.69% computation-deadline misses.

Traceability is part of the contribution. Frontend controls constrain event
order, the backend and firmware validate protocol/state, and versioned
manifests make finalized raw and processed evidence checksum-verifiable. The
furniture case preserves original records while near-equal bidirectional
offsets expose the reference-entry correction; its in-sample corrected
residuals are evidence of consistency rather than independent calibration.

During development and non-finalized RV1103 runs, several operational
interruptions occurred under severe memory pressure. In one inspected case,
the board reported approximately 0.9 MiB free and 2.5 MiB available memory
while `localize_uart` was no longer active and SSH access was unresponsive.
The coincidence strongly indicates a memory-pressure failure, although no
kernel OOM trace was retained to establish whether the OOM killer terminated
the process. Taken together, these observations identify RV1103 memory
capacity as the primary suspected operational limitation. No corresponding
interruption appears in the finalized RV1106 sessions, which is consistent
with, but does not prove, this memory-capacity interpretation. Because the two
targets did not undergo balanced resource testing, the absence of an observed
RV1106 interruption does not establish general platform reliability.

The main limitations are one primary RV1103 board–LiDAR assembly, no integrated
mobile-platform deployment, one indoor environment,
manual placement/object motion, small and unbalanced session counts,
independently acquired cross-board maps and marker references, and dependent
scans. Ground Truth measures one-marker repeatability rather than absolute
surveying accuracy; R2/M4 is unresolved; furniture correction is post hoc and
has no holdout; and RV1106 has no balanced resource comparison. Results are
descriptive, not population probabilities.

# Conclusion

The deployed local–global multi-resolution system connects physical accuracy,
loss recovery, disturbance behavior, ablation, and embedded cost in one
auditable workflow. RV1103 achieved 0.0279 m/0.589° pooled nominal Route RMSE,
recovered all four observed kidnapped cases within 0.970 s, and accepted
99.37% of dynamic-window scans. Only the combined method recovered in both
ablations; its RV1103 matcher P95 was 49–50 ms. Recorded-paced execution used
66.05% time-weighted CPU with 0.69% computation-deadline misses, while live
operation exposed limited inter-scan margin. Global-recovery latency and live
scheduling are the primary optimization targets.

# Data and Code Availability

Finalized project evidence retains raw telemetry, configurations, processed
results, and SHA-256 manifests. Source code and publication materials are
maintained in the
[hharyono/SLAM repository](https://github.com/hharyono/SLAM.git); release
availability is tied to the repository revision cited by the submitted
article.
